title: Speaking Life & Encouragement
subtitle: A bit, a rudder, a fire — and a test you can run first.
objectives: Name the three images James uses for the tongue
Explain why words cannot be unsaid

cards.title: James compares the tongue to machinery
cards.text: Not to niceness. Three images, and all three are about something small that steers or destroys something much larger.

cards.title: A bit, a rudder, a fire
cards.text: Each one makes the same argument from a different angle.
points: **James 3:3** — a bit in a horse's mouth. Small part, large animal.
**James 3:4** — a ship's rudder. Tiny, against wind and weight.
**James 3:5** — a small fire in a forest.
**Disproportionate effect** is the point of all three.

cards.title: Six buttons
cards.text: Tap each image. The last three buttons are what to do about it.

question.text: James 3:4 compares the tongue to a…
question.explain: The smallest control surface sets the course.

cards.title: Three questions, in order
cards.text: Fast enough to run before speaking.
points: **Is it true?**
**Is it needed?**
**Is this the moment?**
**Ephesians 4:29** sets the bar at *building up*, not merely not lying.

question.text: What is the bar set by Ephesians 4:29?
question.explain: Which is higher than merely avoiding falsehood.

cards.title: Name the thing, not the person
cards.text: Vague praise is forgettable and sounds automatic.
points: **"You're great"** carries no information.
**"You kept going after that round"** is a fact.
**A named thing** can be repeated on purpose.
**1 Thessalonians 5:11** — encourage one another, and build each other up.

cards.title: One sentence from a corner changes a round
cards.text: Thirty seconds, and what gets said decides the next three minutes.
points: **"Hands up, two more jabs"** is usable.
**"Come on, do better"** is not.
**Specific instruction, specific encouragement.**
**Same rule in both directions.**

cards.title: A rudder is a tiny control surface
cards.text: Look at the size of a ship's rudder compared with the ship.
points: **A few square metres** turning thousands of tonnes.
**It works because it acts on moving water.**
**Leverage, not force.**
**James chose this image** because it is literally true.

question.text: James compares the tongue to a bit, a fire and a…

cards.title: That is the rudder
cards.alt: The stern of a large ship in dry dock, its single rudder strikingly small beneath the towering hull
cards.text: A few square metres turning thousands of tonnes. James picked it on purpose.

cards.title: Voice chat is the rudder
cards.text: One teammate's tone decides whether the next ten minutes work.
points: **One person calling calmly** holds a team together.
**One person blaming** ends it faster than any mistake.
**Nobody's aim changed.** The words did.
**Disproportionate effect**, exactly as described.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Bit, rudder, fire — small things with disproportionate effect.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 10 Devotion. James compares the tongue to three pieces of machinery, and the week keeps that frame rather than reducing the topic to niceness: all three images are about leverage, something small steering or destroying something far larger. The teardown lens makes the rudder literal, since a few square metres really do turn thousands of tonnes, which is the kind of concrete fact that makes the metaphor stick. Two practical tools come out of it: the three-question test before speaking, and the rule that encouragement names the thing rather than the person. The closing point is honest — an apology repairs a relationship but does not unsay a sentence.
discussion: Ask for the three images and what they have in common.
Ask him to run the three-question test on something he nearly said.
Ask for one specific piece of encouragement for someone today.
Ask what an apology can and cannot do.
extension: Have him give one named, specific encouragement a day for a week.
Have him look up the size of a ship's rudder against the ship.
misconceptions: "Watching your words means saying less." Ephesians 4:29 sets the bar at building up.
"Praise is praise." Vague praise carries no information.
"An apology undoes it." It repairs; it does not unsay.
